title: The body is on loan
hook: Epictetus lists even the body among things not fully ours (Enchiridion 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: other people's opinions, on their side of the line. Your line was theirs to think. Did you hand one back across the table? Day one hundred sixteen.

A friend lends you her car for the weekend, and something changes in the driver's seat. The fries stay in the bag. The mirrors get checked twice. The tank goes back full, maybe after a trip through the car wash. Nobody asked for any of it. A borrowed thing gets a different kind of care. Now here's a strange thought from Epictetus, the last one of our week on control. What if your body is more like the borrowed car than the one you own? Today: the body is on loan.
screen: `A FRIEND'S CAR.` → `NO FRIES, MIRRORS TWICE.` → `WHAT IF THE BODY IS BORROWED?`

segments.voice: Remember the first lines of the Handbook: some things are up to us, some are not. The very first thing on the not-up-to-us list is the body. At first that sounds wrong. My body is the most mine thing there is. But think about it the way Epictetus did. You didn't choose its height, or its genes, or when it catches a cold. You can't order your knee to stop hurting or your hair to stay. It ages on its own schedule. You live in it, you steer it, you're responsible for it. But you don't fully command it. Later in the Handbook, Epictetus gives the picture that goes with this. Never say about anything, I have lost it, he says, in paraphrase; say instead, I have given it back. The things we have are given for a time, like a traveler's room at an inn: use it well while you're there, and don't pretend it's yours forever. Here's the surprise. This isn't a reason to neglect the body. It's the reason to care for it well. The borrowed car gets the careful driving. When the body is on loan, sleep, water, a walk, the vegetables, the checkup: these aren't vanity, and they aren't punishment. They're how a good guest treats a borrowed thing. And the loan helps with the other side too. When the knee hurts or the mirror shows a new gray hair, you can meet it with less outrage. That part was never yours to command. What's yours is how you care for it, and how you meet what it does.
screen: `FIRST ON THE NOT-MINE LIST: THE BODY.` · `YOU STEER IT; YOU DON'T COMMAND IT.` · `NOT LOST: GIVEN BACK.` · `CARE FOR IT LIKE A BORROWED THING.` · then, large: `ON LOAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for your body like a borrowed thing. Settle, and breathe. Move your attention slowly through the body: feet, legs, belly, chest, hands, shoulders, face. Notice it the way you'd look over a borrowed car: with interest, not judgment. Where is it tired? Where does it ache? Then ask: what's one thing a good guest would do for it today? Water, sleep, a stretch, a walk. Choose one. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
The body is on loan. Epictetus puts it among things not fully ours, which is why it deserves careful keeping. Today's word.
screen: `THE BODY IS ON LOAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: on loan. Today, do the one thing a good guest would do for this body. And this week's six lines, from mine or not mine to on loan, all ask the same question. Tomorrow, a new week: gratitude. Day one hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism treat the body as not fully theirs, following Enchiridion 1 and 11: they care for it steadily and try to meet illness and aging without outrage.

myth: Epictetus puts the body among the things up to us
the body is the very first thing on his not-up-to-us list.
Epictetus says to say I have given it back, not I have lost it
the things we have are given for a time.
if the body isn't fully yours, there's no point caring for it
the opposite: Epictetus says to care for it as a thing that belongs to another.

fork.setup: you notice a new ache that won't go away. following this week's Stoic sorting, what do you do?
options: rage at your body for letting you down.
ignore it, since the body isn't yours anyway.
meet it calmly, and do your part: rest, or see a doctor.
fork.reveal: the ache was never yours to command. your care and your response are, so you do your part and let go of the outrage.

original.note: Greek: the body. In Enchiridion 1 it is the first thing on the list of what is not up to us.

trapdoor: what you thought: your body is the one thing that's definitely yours.
what it means: you live in it and steer it, but don't command it, so you care for it like a borrowed thing.
what a scholar hears: σῶμα heads Epictetus's list of things not up to us, and Enchiridion 11 turns loss into giving back.
